title: Structural disorder and critical voltage scaling in Al/AlOx/Al Josephson junction arrays
authors: Amanuel M. Berhane, Susan Coppersmith, Emma Mitchell, Timothy Duty
abstract: The insulating state of one-dimensional Josephson junction (JJ) arrays is governed by collective charge dynamics and disorder-induced pinning, resulting in a finite critical voltage under dc bias. Here, we investigate the influence of fabrication-induced structural defects on the critical-voltage scaling of small-capacitance Aluminium-Aluminium oxide-Aluminium (Al/AlOx/Al) JJ arrays. Controlled variation of the aluminium evaporation rate produces pronounced changes in grain morphology and room-temperature junction resistance. Despite these substantial structural modifications, the normalised critical-voltage scaling is preserved, demonstrating that the collective transport behaviour is remarkably robust against this class of fabrication-induced defects. In contrast, the deliberate introduction of nanoscale gaps into the junctions introduces additional junction-to-junction structural variations that systematically modify the normalised scaling behaviour. Likewise, in situ postfabrication oxidation alters the scaling coefficient while preserving the functional form of the scaling law, indicating that the collective transport is sensitive to specific classes of structural modifications. These results establish which fabrication-induced structural defects influence the collective transport in insulating Al/AlOx/Al Josephson junction arrays, providing new insight into the role of fabrication-induced structural disorder and practical guidance for the design of future Quantum Phase Slip (QPS) devices.
summary: This work examines how structural disorder affects the critical voltage scaling in Josephson junction arrays. By comparing results from varying fabrication parameters (like deposition rate) against those with engineered defects (like nanoscale gaps), the authors map out which structural variations merely renormalize transport coefficients versus those that fundamentally alter the collective pinning physics. This provides crucial design guidelines for superconducting quantum devices.
main_problem: The study investigates how fabrication-induced structural defects influence the critical-voltage scaling in one-dimensional Josephson junction (JJ) arrays.
main_result: The normalized critical-voltage scaling is remarkably robust against variations in aluminum evaporation rates, but the scaling behavior is significantly altered by the deliberate introduction of nanoscale gaps.
method: The authors combine low-temperature transport measurements (IVCs) with structural characterization (SEM) and theoretical analysis based on the pinned Luttinger-liquid theory.
model_or_system: The physical system is Al/AlOx/Al Josephson junction arrays, operating in the insulating regime where transport is governed by collective charge dynamics and disorder-induced pinning.
key_observables:
Critical voltage ($V_C$), room-temperature junction resistance ($R_j$), and the normalized critical-voltage scaling relationship ($
u$ vs. $w$).
important_parameters: Aluminum evaporation rate, junction geometry (Type-AI, Type-BI, Type-BII), and the ratio of Josephson energy to charging energy ($E_J/E_{CP}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the pinned Luttinger-liquid theory to describe the collective transport behavior in the presence of disorder.
figures_summary: Figures show SEM images illustrating morphology changes with deposition rate, $R_j$ dependence on dose, and the collapse of normalized critical-voltage scaling onto a common functional form.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the effects of different structural modifications—varying evaporation rates, post-oxidation, and introducing nanoscale gaps—on the measured critical voltage scaling, contrasting the robustness of the functional form versus the sensitivity of the prefactors.
why_interesting: The robustness of the scaling law despite structural changes suggests underlying universal physics governing collective transport in disordered superconducting systems, which is relevant to understanding quantum phase transitions.
